subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS WITH EUROPEAN COUNTRIES FOR NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question would normally be addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Because of his absence and its importance, may I address it to the Prime Minister? It concerns reports, today, that Canadian negotiators hope to conclude separate bilateral agreements with three European countries as a temporary solution to our uranium export embargo on shipments to the European Common Market. Article 34 of the Treaty of Rome states that "restrictions of exports, and all measures having equivalent effect, shall be prohibited between member states," and Article 54 of the Euratom Treaty clearly lays down the principle of equal access to nuclear resources and the pursuit of a common supply policy. In view of the apparent contradiction between treaty obligations of the European countries and the type of agreement being sought by Canada, could the Prime Minister confirm our new negotiating intent and indicate what form of absolutely ironclad safeguards are possible to block actions by other EEC treaty members to override our bilateral agreements? Also, I wonder if he could say if that would be legally binding.

subtopic: REASON FOR NEGOTIATIONS WITH WEST GERMANY FOR NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS IN VIEW OF SALE OF REPROCESSING PLANT TO BRAZIL
REASON FOR NEGOTIATIONS WITH WEST GERMANY FOR NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS IN VIEW OF SALE OF REPROCESSING PLANT TO BRAZIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is true that the Secretary of State for External Affairs did take notice of this question raised by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands. Specifically, because it is part and parcel of this attempted bilateral agreement, that of resuming sales of nuclear materials to West Germany, and in view of the fact that West Germany is concluding an arrangement to supply a plutonium extraction plant as part of its total fuel cycle provisions for the country of Brazil, a country which has not signed the non-proliferation agreement and which could greatly destabilize the situation in the whole of Latin America, can the Prime Minister indicate for what reasons Canada is pursu-

March 30, 1977
Oral Questions
ing this policy in spite of the strong position taken by President Carter in meetings with the West German representative in Washington?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REASON FOR NEGOTIATIONS WITH WEST GERMANY FOR NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS IN VIEW OF SALE OF REPROCESSING PLANT TO BRAZIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure what the hon. member means when he says "pursuing this policy". Long before President Carter was elected, Canada had taken a very strong stand on safeguards. 1 discussed the matter with almost every European leader that I met and indicated at least three years ago that Canada was taking a very strong stand on this. I attempted to persuade all the other nuclear suppliers that they should come up to the level of safeguards that Canada was contemplating and has since then implemented. Of course we do not have complete authority to run the affairs of other nations, but we do try to persuade them to our point of view. I repeat what I said earlier, the Secretary of State for External Affairs will try to have a report on the particular aspects of the question which the hon. member raised.

subtopic: REASON FOR NEGOTIATIONS WITH WEST GERMANY FOR NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS IN VIEW OF SALE OF REPROCESSING PLANT TO BRAZIL
speechtext: I wonder if the Prime Minister could address directly, because of its major importance, whether Canada has taken any position with regard to West Germany's pursuit of the supply of a reprocessing plant to Brazil, in light of Brazil's unwillingness to sign the non-proliferation treaty and the potential threat of the establishment of that whole nuclear fuel cycle in Brazil. Has the government expressed its opinion to West Germany or is that at all part of the negotiations with respect to resuming bilateral arrangements with that country?

subtopic: REASON FOR NEGOTIATIONS WITH WEST GERMANY FOR NUCLEAR SAFEGUARDS IN VIEW OF SALE OF REPROCESSING PLANT TO BRAZIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know about other ministers and departments but I raised this matter with Chancellor Schmidt. I indicated that I hoped he would come closer to our point of view. We will no doubt have other occasions to discuss this matter together. Of course we are concerned about this. At least three ministers in the House have said that. I repeat, I have personally raised the whole matter of the nuclear question with Chancellor Schmidt as well as other European leaders.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF SAFEGUARD AGREEMENTS AND INQUIRY INTO USE OF NUCLEAR ENERGY

subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF RADIO AND TELEVISION STATIONS BY MR. DESMARAIS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister arising from reports that Mr. Paul Desmarais of Power Corporation has completed negotiations which will lead to the acquisition of six Ontario radio and television stations, thus adding to an empire which through direct or indirect means controls a large number of newspapers including La Presse, the French language paper with the highest circulation in Canada, and extensive radio and TV stations. In the light of the obvious dangers which arise from the concentration of media ownership in a democracy, will the Prime Minister assure the House that he will take direct steps to prevent further concentration of ownership in this field?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF RADIO AND TELEVISION STATIONS BY MR. DESMARAIS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: This would seem to be a question which is either premature or directed to the wrong person. I believe the CRTC would have to authorize any agreement of that kind. Given the exercise of this regulation and regimentation by the CRTC I think it is refreshing to see some Quebec entrepreneurs buying into Ontario for a change.

subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF RADIO AND TELEVISION STATIONS BY MR. DESMARAIS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: So much for the seriousness with which the Prime Minister set up this royal commission on the concentration of corporate ownership. I should like to ask this exponent of corporate imperialism whether, given the fact that it is precisely through a series of such decisions which have already been made in the past by the CRTC which have permitted this concentration of power in media ownership, the right hon. gentleman does not think it is an important requirement of his obligation as Prime Minister in a democracy to make it clear that the government does not favour the concentration of ownership in this field?

speechtext: I am not aware of the facts the hon. member is discussing. I will take note of them on behalf of the minister. I am sure that if the minister is able to get the information the hon. member is talking about she will be able to comment on it. It has made decisions in the past, and permitted it-that is the whole point of my question. Considering that seven years ago the Senate committee on the mass media stated that newspapers and broadcasting stations were "pulling the maximum out of their communities and giving back the minimum in return", and that "the concentration of media ownership has proceeded to the point at which some form of intervention by the state is desirable and necessary", and since these opinions come from a committee of the Senate headed by an old friend of the Prime Minister, I should like to ask the right hon. gentleman whether he will not take immediate steps, in advance of the report of the royal commission

which is looking into corporate power, in order that further concentration of media ownership might be avoided?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries. subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN NUMBER OF GUARDIANS ON SALMON RIVERS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that in this time of restraint and at a time when we are trying to stretch every dollar, we will not be able to spend much more money in the area mentioned by the hon. member. subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN NUMBER OF GUARDIANS ON SALMON RIVERS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister mentioned restraint in spending. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON TWO-LICENCE SYSTEM FOR FISHERMEN ON WEST COAST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, after representations from and discussions with the hon. member and his colleagues from British Columbia as well as members from across the floor, I have decided to delay the application of these changes in the licensing program for one year. The House resumed, from Tuesday, March 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cullen that Bill C-27, to establish the department of employment and immigration, the Canada employment and immigration commission and the Canada employment and immigration advisory council, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, and to amend certain other statutes in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I continue my line of discussion of yesterday evening I should like to set the record straight with regard to what the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) raised during the question period. He quoted a paper which meant to quote something I had said. He did not identify the source and I shall not try to contradict that source, but I should just like to set the record straight. I never pretended or intended to speak for other MPs whether from the Atlantic provinces or elsewhere.
It is a matter of public knowledge that members on this side of the House are concerned about some of the provisions of Bill C-27.
I was asked by a series of reporters about my concerns. I stated what those concerns were. I was also asked whether
Employment and Immigration
other Atlantic MPs felt like that, and I said it was a matter of public knowledge that others did. They asked me how many Atlantic members there were. I said that was a matter of fact. There are 13, but I do not speak for the others; they are very capable of speaking for themselves. That I should have said that the government was looking again at Bill C-27 and its implications is not news. The minister himself said last week- I think he stated it in the House-that the government is looking again at some of the provisions of the bill.

Last evening, when the House adjourned, I was speaking on some positive aspects of the bill, Mr. Speaker. I was saying that I could support the bill on second reading because it has some potentially positive aspects, particularly as far as the integration of UIC offices and manpower centres is concerned. I say this can be positive because it can be a step towards the structural change which I hope will occur in the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I said last evening. As far as we are concerned, those of us who come from areas with a high level of unemployment recognize that in some areas of the country, and even in our areas, people are concerned about the unemployment insurance system. In fact there are moral and attitudinal problems throughout the country. Some people abuse the system, both at the employer and employee level, and we know that this situation cannot be maintained, that we must do something. What we suggest is that, in changing this situation, we should be careful to avoid hurting people in high unemployment areas who have no chance to work.

I shall repeat that in English because I think it is important. I agree, and a lot of others agree, that there are moral and attitudinal problems with the unemployment insurance program. We know there are people who decide not to work or who leave their jobs voluntarily, and we know that the program generally is abused and misused by employers and employees. What we are saying is that the way to remedy this is to change drastically the administrative structure of the UIC, not to take the risk of hurting people in high unemployment areas who have no chance to work.
We are concerned about two provisions of the bill. One has to do with the increase in the qualifying period and the other with changes in the benefit structure. I deplore the fact that most of those who have spoken about this bill, including members of the opposition, have apparently not noted what the changes in the benefit structure would mean for those on the minor entitlement side, those with minor attachment to the labour force. Obviously, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), the hon. member for Hamilton West, and other hon. members whose speeches I have heard or read have failed to note that the change in the benefit structure affecting those in the areas of highest unemployment would mean that claimants could lose up to three months of benefit.
The Conservative spokesman, the hon. member for St. John's East, said they would put forward amendments in

March 30, 1977
Employment and Immigration
committee. As I have said before in this chamber, I believe their amendment really reflects the fact that their party cannot take a united stand, because up to now they have not suggested that the period should remain at eight weeks in certain regions of the country according to law. What they are saying is that the governor in council should have the power to do this. That is skating on both sides of the issue just to enable them to go into the Atlantic provinces and say, "We wanted it to remain eight weeks. It was the government that didn't want it. We wanted the government to have the authority". If the Conservative opposition believes the period should remain at eight weeks in certain parts of the country, or that it should not be 12 weeks, let them say so and present amendments in committee or in the House at report stage. Then we will do that within the law.

speechtext: The hon. member says I should stick to the bill. I am sticking to the bill. I should like to go to another part of my speech, since my time is limited, and deal with this myth that those on unemployment insurance at frequent times during the year are freeloaders or loafers.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Tell your minister that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not condemning those who say this, because as a politician I am sensitive to what people in other parts of the country feel and I think their questions have to be answered. That is our duty. But some people do feel that unemployment insurance is a means of living for some people, a means to enable them to meet the family budget. As the Economic Council of Canada has said, unemployment insurance is the most effective instrument in the fight against poverty that this country has seen.
I want the unemployment insurance program to remain such. I believe that in this country, which in the world context is a rich country, we should fight poverty and I do not think we should be afraid to maintain programs toward that end. Areas like mine, which are like most areas of the Atlantic provinces, suffer from chronic unemployment which has reached a very high level, and this provision to reduce the qualifying period could have disastrous effects, as could the changes in the benefit structure. While I will support the bill on second reading, I believe the bill can be changed if the House of Commons wants to change it. There are some good first steps in the bill, such as the integration of the two services. I have been told that other members on this side-and, I hope, members on the other side-will continue the fight in committee and at report stage to change these two provisions.
I have heard that there could be a variable entrance scheme. I am not all that concerned about that so long as areas like mine in northeastern New Brunswick and areas in the Atlantic provinces generally are not badly hit by this change from 8 to 12 weeks.
I do not condemn people who believe this myth about the UIC, because they do not know better. If they did, they probably would not say that. The fact is that in some areas of high unemployment unemployment insurance has become a way of life for some people. This does not mean that they are lazy, that they are loafers or freeloaders. What it means is that they have only short-term employment. They have decided to live in that particular area, and the unemployment insurance program is a means of helping them to remain there. This country is concerned about national unity. It is a society that has said that as much as possible people should have the opportunity of living and working in the area of their choice. It seems to me that if we accept this we must pay the price.
A lot of people who are caught up in this cycle of unemployment insurance and short-term employment could work for longer periods. But what we have to ask ourselves is, under what conditions are they working? Through its framework of labour laws at the provincial and federal level this country has accepted a certain standard of work. Through collective bargaining workers can bargain for better conditions, more leisure time and that sort of thing. What is so wrong about people who are unorganized using something like UIC to improve their standards?
I meet people in my constituency office, indeed in every part of my constituency, who have left their employment with just
March 30, 1977

cause. In some other parts of the country, such as Ontario and British Columbia, and even in some parts of Quebec, labour unions are well organized and strong and have fought politically and economically for better working conditions for their members. If they saw working conditions in some other parts of the country, they would not work there. So let us approach this debate from that perspective. It is not a case of people leaving well-paid jobs to go on unemployment insurance. I have never met one person in my constituency or anywhere in my province on the UIC short-term employment cycle who was in that situation by choice. These people find themselves in that situation for historical and cultural reasons.
To give the House an example, Mr. Speaker, in my home town the government helped the community build a senior citizens' home. Workers at senior citizens' homes in New Brunswick have a union. They also know that they will be required to work just about every day, even in the wintertime and even if there is no public transportation. They have to make their own transportation arrangements. In my home area of Tracadie, with a population of about 3,000, there were openings for 34 or 35 people at this senior citizens' home. The general unemployment rate at certain times of the year in the town can be as high as 40 per cent. Since it is a small town, applications were received from persons within a radius of 30 miles.
Do you know how many applications were received for these 35 jobs, Mr. Speaker? There were over 430 applications from people who were ready to drive both summer and winter, day in and day out, to this senior citizens' home to work difficult shifts, sometimes from midnight to eight, sometimes from four to midnight, with no public transportation facilities. How can we say that people do not want to work? People do want to work, but there is no employment. People have accepted that as a way of life.
I am not saying there are no abuses. Since we went on the defensive in 1971 and the pressure is on to deliver UIC cheques, it is easy to cheat, I agree. But do not cut people off unemployment insurance at the base level of 8 or 12 weeks. Do not change the benefit structure to cut them off. The fact is that we have to accept that unemployment insurance is not being administered as the law provides. When this parliament passed the legislation and the amendments it could not foresee that implementation would be so difficult that the present situation would arise.
I believe that integration is a good step. As for dealing with the moral problem of those who cheat, those who are not motivated to work, we live in a pretty liberal society, a very advanced society, and we cannot deal with those not motivated to work by using a stick or by kicking them in the pants. Motivating these people to work should be done positively, sensitively and humanly.
I have a suggestion in principle: I would like to see the Unemployment Insurance Commission changed. I also have a suggestion for some change in the UIC administration and its
Employment and Immigration
implementation. It would be consistent and compatible with this advanced society in some parts of the country which have given the framework of negotiation for workers in order to obtain better working conditions and salaries. That relationship is not only economical but sometimes it is political. We should be able to do that in every labour district with respect to integration. We have computers, and we should have people who know how to run computers and to program them. There is no reason why we do not have a job inventory in every labour district. There is no reason why we cannot update this information every three months so we can have an indication on file of the jobs available in an area.
Perhaps the law will have to be changed. The administration should be such that when a claimant applies for a position we should have on file his profile; we should have on file his age. You could ask him all the information you want about his training and his background. We should match that application with the job inventory and see if there is a job available in that area. If there is not, you can say to the person, "I am sorry; you have to look for a job", and you try to help him look for a job or put him on training. You can also say, "There are job openings in Sudbury, the Yukon or British Columbia that pay $10 an hour. Would you like to take a training course? We can help you to go there." You cannot start with force. You cannot say, "You have to go." There are ways to motivate people. Most of the young people will respond to that. Those who are not established with a mortgage on their homes, and those who are not attached to the community may want to do that.
If you start giving powers to officials to make a job inventory and you cut people off more quickly, as we are doing with increased benefit control, that is not so bad. I do not mind that as long as those people have a relatively quick and sensible human appeal system. The appeal systems for UIC and the Department of National Revenue are totally inadequate. In my home town I have cases of 200 suspensions between November and December on insurability. As of today, March 30, 86 of them have not yet been dealt with. That is incredible; that is not a way to treat people. The appeal system has to be drastically changed and brought down to the community.
The problem of people deciding to stay on UIC, or people going bn UIC presents us with a moral and attitudinal problem. If you want to make a judgment on that, and if you are going to start cutting people off, I would say go ahead and give the onus of the doubt to the officials. In almost every community, or at least within 25 miles of where the population justifies it, an appeal system should be available. I do not think you should put an appeal system in every isolated corner of the country. In communities where the population justifies it, there should be an appeal system available if a judgment was made by an insensitive official on the side of the job inventory or on the side of a decision to exclude a claimant from benefits.
The appeal system should consist of people from the community who will know the claimant so that they can make a judgment on the moral question and on the question of atti-

March 30, 1977
Employment and Immigration
tude. They can make that judgment only at the community level. If you have to drive 60 miles, 100 miles or 150 miles to get to an appeal board as exists in some parts of the country, there is not only a question of economy-the cost of travelling which is an important factor for some people-but also the people there do not necessarily know the person. That is why we are so concerned about increasing the benefit control. If we increase it, we have to make sure that the appeal system is made more sensitive and is humanized.
This bill attempts to redress the balance between what is paid in and what is paid out of the UIC. The minister has said he wants to protect the integrity of the program. I agree with him that the integrity of the program should be protected. We are dealing with public funds and we are dealing with funds that workers pay out of their pay-cheques, and we have to be careful about how that money is spent. The changes we bring about should not be changes that will hurt people. There is a possibility to administer this program in a way that will be human, sensitive and under which people will not abuse it so that we get the freeloaders and the cheaters out. In theory I agree with protecting the credibility of the program. I agree with redressing the balance between what is paid in and what is paid out.
Hon. members should note that all the criticism they hear about people being on the UIC rolls and all the criticism they hear about their neighbours, friends, daughters and cousins being freeloaders will not be dealt with in this bill. By passing this bill we will not have dealt with the problems of abuse. Hon. members should note that and remind themselves of it. All that will be done by this bill is that we will go forward in trying to improve its administration. That will not be far enough, in my view; but we run the risk of hurting a lot of people with the qualifying period and in the benefit structure.
I conclude by referring to an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of Monday, March 28, 1977. I was going to write a letter to the editor, but I did not have a chance because I was too busy dealing with UIC cases and all types of cases in my constituency office. I shall read the last two paragraphs to underline the misunderstanding and misconception in some parts of the country about the kind of problem with which we are confronted. The last two paragraphs of this editorial read as follows:
If parliament takes these steps it would weed out, not cheaters-what most of these people are doing is within the law-
That is not true, first of all.
-but many who do not qualjfy for unemployment insurance benefits because they do not seek steady employment. All workers know some of these people, and resent them. Also cut off would be some people who want and need work and cannot find it; but welfare benefits would be available to them.
Canada can concentrate its UIC money on those who have worked to earn it, or it can spread it more thinly-robbing some who have worked to earn it-to cover people who haven't. In spite of all the rhetoric about compassion, it's as unpleasantly simple as that.
It is incredible that a newspaper like the Globe and Mail would so misconstrue the situation. As I said earlier in my remarks, I do not blame them for having this kind of attitude. They do not understand. This society, because it is very

generous and liberal, has put into effect programs like welfare and UIC because it wants to distribute income. The wage structure or the work structure in this country does not ensure a fair distribution of income by itself.
Anyone from the Atlantic provinces and from the rural areas of this country knows that the welfare program is an attack on the dignity of human beings. People do not want to be on welfare. By taking people off the welfare rolls and giving them work for eight weeks and giving them UIC, you have made contact with them. You have put them in contact with the labour force, UIC officials and, hopefully, with Canada Manpower officials. Then there is a chance to save them. The Globe and Mail is correct. For a lot of people who are affected, welfare payments would be available to them, but the people do not want welfare.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: They want jobs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
A lot of the people who are affected by this program are poor people who want jobs. Whether it is real or psychological is not important to me. They want at least psychological confidence that they can get what they have worked for-and they are entitled to that. I mentioned that in my home town there are 430 applications for 35 hard working jobs. People want to work. In my view, unemployment insurance and medicare are two pillars of the social security system of this country. They are the two instruments which have fought poverty and deprivation, and I do not want these programs to be changed or tightened up to the extent that their intention, which was to help the little people of this country, is changed.
It has been said that the government would compensate the losses of funds with an infusion of funds into job creation. First, it is impossible to guarantee that those who will get the jobs will be the people who are affected. Nobody can give that guarantee. Anyone who knows how the administration of Canada Manpower centres and the administration of job creation programs works knows that it is impossible to guarantee that on an individual basis. Second, there is no trade-off. There is no compensation of funds, because the saving of unemployment insurance is unknown. It is unknown because the job creation fund sometimes takes people off UIC rolls and puts them to work at a wage lower than the amount they receive from the UIC.
I am not saying that is bad. If we put people to work and if we pay them a little less, that is all right, provided it is acceptable employment. But the saving of unemployment insurance benefits is unknown because we do not know exactly what the people we take off the UIC rolls were receiving in UIC benefits and what they will be paid under the Canada Works program or under LIP. In my view, if the government wants to reduce unemployment it should put funds into job creation and there would be an automatic unemployment insurance benefit saving. If we come up with effective job creation programs, UIC money will automatically be saved.
March 30, 1977

Instead of putting the cart before the horse, we should put the horse before the cart and then everything would be fine.
I repeat that I will support this bill at second reading because I think there are some good provisions in it, but I will continue making representations and doing all I can to get the bill changed in committee. If it is not changed in committee to take care of these two provisions, we will make sure it is brought back to the House at report stage so that the House can decide if it wants these two provisions-which could be harmful to people-to pass.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the government is basing its success on the principle that the third try is the lucky one. Much time and money was wasted on the previous two changes in unemployment insurance provisions. There can be little doubt that weaknesses and loopholes have mounted instead of diminishing. I believe that one of the first things the government did when it was elected in 1972 was change the unemployment insurance system. At that time there was a ceiling on the amount the government could pay into the fund of $800 million. We thought it was a mistake then to take that ceiling off. We still think it would be a mistake because we can no longer hold the government accountable for the tax money, revenues and income which go into the unemployment insurance fund.
It seems to me that accountability is the key word here whether it applies to the government, individuals or others who pay into the unemployment insurance fund or receive benefits from it. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) just mentioned that this bill would not deal with abuses. I would like to deal with some of the areas of abuse of unemployment insurance because I think we have to recognize what they are and where they are before we can deal properly with them. I am not satisfied with the way the unemployment insurance system operates within our economy. That is not because of the people who administer it, because I know they have a very difficult job, but I think we as Canadians are making a great mistake today because we try to end too many of our problems by confrontation rather than by conciliation. If ever a system of confrontation was set up by a government, it was the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The hon. member for Gloucester himself said that in his town there have been 200 suspensions. That just means that people are going against the system. They are confronting one another and causing problems. The Unemployment Insurance Commission will not operate satisfactorily until the government of the day or a succeeding government comes up with a whole new concept of what unemployment insurance should be. At the present time everybody is angry. The 200 people who have been suspended are angry. There are thousands of people like that across the country, and thousands of people who pay into the fund continuously from January 1 to December 31 year in and year out, are angry because it is just another financial burden on them.
In this government's term of office it has destroyed more incentive in this country than had been destroyed in the previous 100 years. This country was built on incentive and
Employment and Immigration
pride, and this government has done its best to destroy that in the last ten years. In a great many cases this is also happening to our unemployment insurance system. It is difficult to criticize people who have paid into the fund year in and year out and who decide that they want to get back some of the money they paid. Those people think they have a right to it. The government should come up with a plan to create an incentive so that sometime down the road those people would realize that there would be an advantage for them to leave their money in and not use it. If we could do that, they would go out and find work. These people should be encouraged to stay off unemployment insurance benefits rather than encouraged to feel that collecting is their right because they have paid into it.
We have to take a look at all the shortcomings of the operations of the commission in order to arrive at a solution to the problems. This jacking around from eight to twelve weeks and back and forth is not the only solution, but it is a move in the right direction. There is no doubt about that because our economy cannot withstand the heavy load which is placed upon it. Many people are being paid not to work, and in our geographical location where we have four, five and six months of winter and where some of us have to work in the summertime, it is difficult for some to work 12 months of the year. However, there are some people in our society who make as much in six, seven or eight months as others who work 12 months and pay into the fund continuously.
1 believe the latter have a grievance, and until some incentive is built into the system there will be a great deal of dissatisfaction with it. If unemployment insurance is in fact insurance, it should protect against loss of work. In other words, should an employee be out of work for some reason beyond his control-because he was fired, because a business or other operation ceased, because of insufficient work or some other reasonable reason-he should be protected by insurance. However, to some degree this program has worked in reverse and has protected unwilling workers who have quit jobs without just cause as soon as they qualified for benefits or shortly thereafter or who have had little or no intention of working on a continuous basis. In some cases something has happened to destroy the desire to earn a living, to take away the natural initiative and pride in those joining the work force for the first time, and to discourage the legitimate, hardworking Canadians who take pride in themselves and their jobs and in providing for their families.
Regardless of the initial employment requirement for eligibility, regardless of the training provided, regardless of the limits placed on the premiums and benefits paid, the root of most of the difficulty is that people have been misled and encouraged to believe that they are entitled to insurance and to live by that rule.
Far be it for me to imply that the majority of people follow that practice. I am talking about those who work for and live by the unemployment insurance regulations. Instead of unemployment insurance being a protection, as is insurance against
4486

March 30, 1977
Employment and Immigration
fire, accident, ill health or death, it has become part of a life pattern. The federal government is more to blame for this than any other body in Canada. Can we place the blame on the workers who fall into that category when emphasis is put on how and when a person can qualify instead of on how to find work, how to retain work, how to make work for oneself to earn a livelihood, how to train for a job, and how students should work toward a higher education?
I will deal with that question later in my speech. Today the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) started whining and complaining about students not being able to find employment before the majority of them look around, put a pen to paper or a foot to the ground to find if work is available. What do they do? Surely they do not just question the Prime Minister and wait to see what the government and the taxpayer will do for them. In my opinion the thinking of government has been turned backward into stagnation. The government is prepared to allow a welfare state to develop, instead of following the true and tried principles of teaching and allowing people to earn a living and to do their own thinking, which is necessary-and I emphasize that-to develop a certain quality of life which the pioneers of this country have worked for and developed.
There is another group of able-bodied workers whose training has mainly been to figure out if it is more rewarding, dollarwise, to work or to go on welfare, to qualify for insurance benefits and to quit. Then there is the great majority of those who are prepared to improve and who merit better pay and fringe benefits, such as more holidays and sick leave, a promotion with added responsibility and the wonderful feeling of being a responsible, ongoing citizen able to provide for himself, to help his country and to care for his family.
People who have lost this sense of pride usually are unhappy and wayward, and life has lost its meaning for them. We cannot blame them entirely. The young people of today have not known life without unemployment insurance and other government doles. They do not realize that they are expected to work to earn a living as did their fathers and grandfathers. The government laid and hatched this bad egg-the new workers are its victims.
In addition to the deprivation which such easy living causes the followers of this pattern of life, the economy of the entire country is feeling the impact. Does this government have any idea of the frustration, discouragement, futility of effort, futility of investment by businesses and industry which, after investing huge amounts of capital and, in some cases, spending years of hard work and planning, find that either they cannot find trained or experienced workers or that employees work for only six or eight weeks and then quit? As examples I would cite the construction industry and auto body shops. In these two areas, as everyone here knows, staff requirements change from day to day, often by leaps and bounds.
How can contracts be met without adequate workers? Besides the cost of paying unemployment benefits to these short-term workers, the contractor and the garage owner sustain a loss which eventually is paid by the public. If we are going to say that lack of trained personnel is the cause of the
[Mr. Towers.)
shortage of permanent staff, there must be something wrong with the Manpower training program. Why can it not be scaled according to area and demand? Can we not ensure that the trainees have a permanent trade in mind when they enroll for a course and that a follow-up course is available to ensure they are channelled into work where their services are needed?
Training is useless if it is only another stopgap for those who want to be paid for putting in time for being taught something which they do not intend to put to use to earn their livelihood. Manpower training must be organized, administered and spelled out following consultation with business and industry so it is dependable, useful and sound economically.
The amendments to the unemployment insurance program, including those proposed in the legislation before us, have failed to take into account lifetime workers who have contributed to the program since its inception and have never collected benefits and who, under the existing rules, receive at retirement a lump sum totalling three weeks insurance. I agree that insurance is supposed to be a payment for protection, but why should employees who do not collect benefits continue to pay through the nose for the short-term, seasonal workers?
I suggest that premiums be scaled in accordance with the number of years of contributions, the total number of claims filed and of benefits paid. In that way a person who has paid into the fund for a certain number of years, say 15 years, should be allowed to withdraw completely from the program but would receive benefits at a time of his choice. By the same token, a worker who works for a certain time and then stops, and works again and stops, should have his premiums scaled upwards. If he knows it is to his advantage to continue to be in the labour force, he will be less likely to take his job casually.
An alternative suggestion would be to inform the continuous worker who has not made a claim, or who has filed one only when thrown out of work through no fault of his own, that on retirement he will receive a certain percentage of his contributions. That would provide an incentive for all workers, be they industrious or otherwise, to work toward a benefit based on an excellent work record. When the driver of a motor vehicle is involved in a certain number of accidents, his premium is increased simply because a private company cannot operate if it has to finance that type of risk. Why should Canadian taxpayers be compelled to finance bad risk workers who float along on premiums paid by legitimate workers? We must create incentive, but we must also exercise justice and provide sensible economic management.
Would it not be possible to encourage the industrious, continuous, dedicated worker by putting in place a program for the protection of the constant worker, thus letting everyone know that his contributions are for insurance against the risk of being put out of work, of being laid off, of having a job discontinued, instead of allowing the unwilling workers, however small may be the number, to collect insurance because they have met the minimum requirements and in this way develop a pattern of living? This parliament should come up with an unemployment insurance program which does not
March 30, 1977

include the word "unemployment" but which will do the job that is required for the Canadian people.
I recognize that regional disparities exist in our country and that there are certain areas which are having serious unemployment problems. This is a grievous situation and therefore the whole system must be tightened up when jobs are scarce. At present, over one million Canadians are unemployed. If ever there is a time when the unemployment insurance program needs tightening up, this is not it. It should be undertaken when the economy is buoyant, not when it is in a recession as at present, because this is going to create a number of problems for a great number of people.
Nevertheless, we must realize that our economy will be in worse difficulty if we continue to pay out $3.5 billion or $4 billion per year, regardless of where it comes from. Rather than continue to pay this kind of money to keep people from working, we would be better to devise a system to encourage people to get into the work force.
I recognize that the government has short-changed people in several parts of Canada, primarily the maritimes. At present we are paying an unprecedented price for oil. As we become more and more dependent upon offshore oil, which is very costly, it seems ridiculous to have one million people unemployed, especially when there is ample coal that could be used for heating homes and developing energy. There are other means to develop heat and energy that would use labour, so it would seem to be in our interests to develop those industries. We just cannot continue to have a $4 billion or $5 billion deficit in the balance of trade each year, especially when we are borrowing money on the foreign market. That will break our economy, and if that happens we will know what real suffering is. Now is the time to take action, when we are still in a position to be able to manoeuvre to some degree.
We all remember the power of Great Britain not many years ago. It was said that Britain ruled the waves and that the sun never set on the British empire. Yet that same British empire, Mr. Speaker, had to go down on its knees to the International Monetary Fund to borrow $3.9 billion. When you consider that we borrowed $8 billion on the United States market last year, it makes you stop and think. It rests with the government to ensure that Canada does not find itself in the same position as Great Britain.
Late as it is, programs should be established to realize the potential of the Canadian people. When the tar sands project was in the early stages, the manager of that huge complex was in a quandary about where he could find personnel with the technical ability required. He told some of us that he would have to go to the United States, Germany and Great Britain to find people with the needed technical abilities. Mr. Speaker, it is not reasonable to suppose that the Canadian people have any less ability than people anywhere else in the world, but perhaps we have not had the initiative, the opportunity nor the desire to use their abilities. The problem may be with Syncrude today, but it will happen with other projects tomorrow.
Employment and Immigration
We must have the foresight to provide the technical people needed on these projects.
I have here a clipping from a recent edition of the Red Deer Advocate and I should like to put a few excerpts on the record. Referring to Miss Trudeau, head of the English department at the high school, the report says:
She told the trustees English teachers were frustrated by the problems created by their large classes and heavy workload.
Arguing for more teachers and smaller classes in the English program, Miss Trudeau said the situation places "an incredible strain" on instructors.
Especially difficult, she said, was the problem of teachers who know they are not accomplishing what they think they should.
"That may be the worst kind of strain of all," she added.
The trustees were responsive to Miss Trudeau's presentation, but said the issue is one of priorities.
That is exactly what I was asking, Mr. Speaker. What are the priorities? The article reports, later:
Superintendent Bill Brownlee said it may be that the student to teacher ratios in vocational courses will have to be increased to allow for smaller classes in the academic courses.
Mr. Speaker, under the Diefenbaker government a program of vocational training was introduced and Red Deer was privileged to have one of the first vocational schools in Canada. I want to stress the value of that program. We know that everybody cannot be an academic, so we must help people in the technical field to get the training for work that will keep this country rolling. The article quotes board chairman, Frances Craigie as saying:
I think we have to look at this right from the elementary level.
Provincial governments have authority for education, but I think there should be negotiation between the federal and provincial levels to encourage learning institutions to make sure that graduates will be useful to society. What use is there in teaching something that is not going to be of benefit to students in later years? Thirteen industrial education graduates will emerge from the University of Alberta this year, but that is not enough in this technical age.
One of the teachers I spoke to about the newspaper article I referred to earlier is very concerned because he has to cope with far too many pupils. In a shop project the maximum number of people gathered around a motor or anything else should be five or six. With a number beyond that, those on the outer edge either cannot see or hear or perhaps do not understand what is being taught. It is better to have situations where teachers do not feel frustrated and pupils have a chance of learning if they are to be useful to society and industry in the future.
Not very long ago I spoke to the manager of a garage who could not find anyone to do the body work, a highly paid occupation. In a shop where six or ten people would ordinarily be required, he had only three. He said they were just not available; he did not have them. At the same time, one million in Canada are unemployed. We must consider this question seriously and come to grips with it, otherwise we shall continue drifting and get into even greater difficulty. Somewhere down the road the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. 80012 -6H

March 30, 1977
Employment and Immigration
Cullen) will be forced to bring in new unemployment insurance regulations, to cope with an economic slowdown. Our unemployment insurance program is like a matchbox, held up by matches; sometimes a match falls down, and the minister must replace it with another match, or program, to stop the entire structure from collapsing.
We must also consider negotiations between labour and management. In this connection I bring to the attention of the House a resolution passed at the annual meeting of the Federated Co-op on June 28, 1976. Copies were sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and the governments of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I shall put the resolution on record because its movers went to great lengths to make suggestions they felt would help labour, management and government in negotiations and efforts to avert strikes. It reads:
Whereas strikes and/or lockouts in services and industries .continue to cause serious damage directly to many sectors of the economy and indirectly to every citizen;
And whereas such strikes and lockouts are making domestic and foreign customers doubtful of our ability to produce and deliver on schedule;
And whereas such loss of confidence diverts buyers elsewhere, resulting in the loss of markets and thus job opportunities for Canadians;
And whereas lockouts, strikes and prolonged periods without contracts create bitterness, loss of confidence between sides and a lack of appreciation one side for the other, leading to a reduced quality of life and productivity at work; Therefore be it resolved that we urge the federal and provincial governments to set up a system of courts where all unsettled negotiations involving services or industries would be settled if collective bargaining were not successful soon after a contract expired (say 30 days);
And be it further resolved that while such collective bargaining or court action was proceeding there would be no interruptions to business or services by either party.
Members on all sides say that strikes lead to lost productivity, hardship for labour and the creation of indirect unemployment. Therefore, we must consider ways to avoid strikes and lockouts. Let me put on record the Co-op's reasons for putting forward the resolution just quoted. They are as follows:
Labour and management in too many important areas seem to have come to the point where negotiations are an ongoing power struggle, where each regards the other as an adversary rather than as a partner dependent on each other. It would appear that each expects the other to bring forth a proposal that is far left of centre so they in turn have to be equally far right. Each side then appears reluctant to be the first to move for fear that move will be taken as a sign of weakness, so we see both sides moving slowly and reluctantly every inch of the way toward centre.
We think also that for the same reason it may well be almost impossible for either side to bring forth a different method to settle deadlocked negotiations, plus the likelihood that if one side were to do so the other would suspect it of being a means of gaining an advantage.
Governments are, we think, in the position of being one of the adversaries because they are the largest employer in the country.
It would appear then that a third party as neutral as possible will have to be responsible for bringing an alternative before the government and country. We believe the co-op body here to be as broad a cross-section of people as it is possible to find in Canada and puts us in the position of being able to and indeed having a responsibility to render Canada and ourselves a real service.
We think that Canadians generally have faith in our courts to deal fairly and resolutely in such matters (for example) damage suits, and could easily be adapted to deal with all aspects of industrial relations.

Those are the words of a non-political body which is sincerely trying to suggest a policy of benefit to all Canadians. I assume that many paying unemployment insurance premiums, and many others collecting benefits, belong to the co-operative movement. Therefore, I hope the Prime Minister will seriously consider the resolution passed by the Federated Co-op in western Canada. As I have said, we cannot go on increasing spending on unemployment insurance. The money comes from all segments of society. I notice that this year the programs administration costs will rise 24 per cent. The problem will keep snowballing until it is stopped.
I come from Alberta, but that does not mean I do not sympathize with the problems of working people. The Globe and Mail of Tuesday, March 29-yesterday-on the front page of the Report On Business section, printed an article about Red Deer, the headline of which reads, "Red Deer prospers amid unprecedented economic growth". Some people feel they will get jobs automatically if they go to Red Deer. That may not be quite true, although there is employment available in the area. Let me read part of the article. It says:
Three demi-clad young men in late model cars bearing Manitoba licence plates rolled up shortly after noon to inquire about accommodation. They had arrived the previous day and two of them promptly found work with an oilfield contractor. The third expected to the 'fixed up' with some kind of job, "paying good money," that some afternoon.
According to them, jobs are plentiful but finding rental accommodation proves much harder and 'when you find something you have to pay three times as much for it as in Brandon.'
Nevertheless, the youths hoped to "make out okay," planning to "stick around to make a few bucks," as labourers in the expanding local work force.
That article exactly illustrates my position on unemployment insurance. There are jobs for people willing to go out to get them. People who go to Red Deer looking for work may run into other problems. In this connection I want to quote part of an article printed in the Advocate of Wednesday, February 23, 1977. It is written by George Yackulic, formerly a member of the press Gallery, and reads:
Alberta's booming economy is attracting a creeping unemployment problem from other parts of Canada, a survey this week indicates...
But some of the newcomers, especially those without special skills or training, are not landing jobs . ..
Mr. Mulhall-
He is the manager of the Red Deer Canada Manpower centre:
-says the jobless ranks here are certainly greater now than a year ago ...
Provincial welfare officials explain that, having been on social assistance back home, some of the newcomers arrive destitute.
"We are getting a lot of them seeking social assistance," an official in Red Deer says. "They are as flat as can be and desperately need help" ...
Many of those complaining are skilled tradesmen but they do not have union standing.
The next part I shall quote has to do with the ethylene plant being built in the area:
Hiring of workers for that project is done through the respective unions for electricians, pipefitters, plumbers, carpenters, labourers, and so on, the unions in turn having waiting lists.
March 30, 1977

Union officials say they are not rejecting qualified prospective members. However, joining a union can be costly for a job-seeker on welfare back home and in Alberta with little money.
For instance, to get on the waiting list of the construction labourer's union, a man must pay that union a fee of $106 ...
Last week more than 60 men anxiously sought jobs at a downtown site where construction is just starting for an apartment building. They represented most of the building trades. But with only preparatory work underway at the site, there was need at the time for only the job superintendent and two young laborers.
Employers in other industries and businesses in the city and district tell of being "swamped" by job-seekers.
Often there is a lack of the required skill or experience needed for a waiting job.
That is the crux of my whole speech. There may be jobs in certain places. The reason they cannot be filled is that those applying do not have the required skill or ability to qualify. We have a great many problems in the whole unemployment situation. As a member of parliament, I have a responsibility to make a contribution. I hope I can do that in a forthright, straightforward manner and that it will be accepted as such by the minister, because we have to come to grips with this problem.
There is no other body in Canada which can do as much, if it has the wish, desire and incentive, as the federal government. I mentioned earlier that we have lost our incentive and pride. We have to turn this around so that Canadian society can enjoy the benefits that can be ours, should be ours, have been enjoyed by past generations and will continue to be ours.
