speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In closing, I urge the government to initiate new plans and programs which will do away with those hardships which we must resolve. If governments will not do that, how can we expect business and unions to do it? We have three main components in our society today: big government, big business and big unions. While I do not like to have government in business, nevertheless I feel it is the responsibility of governments, both federal and provincial, to establish an atmosphere and climate which will be conducive to business establishing programs that will not only be beneficial to business but to the people of this country. In order for benefits to accrue to the people of this country we must have a healthy business community.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as everybody knows, Bill C-27 is intended to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971. Unfortunately this bill as a whole contains very few suggestions to provide the unemployed and those who look for jobs with a glimmer of hope to improve their situation, without losing any pride or human dignity. On one hand, the unemployment curve going upward, their
Employment and Immigration
chances of finding a job are almost nil. On the other hand, the number of weeks of employment is increased from eight to 12 weeks to get qualified for benefits.
After 12 weeks of employment, either because of lack of work or any other reason, the one who is obliged to apply for unemployment insurance is forced to meet the various regulations which too often, due to regional disparities, cannot be put into effect in some region. That bill was introduced December 9, 1976. Today, March 30, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) sets a time limit for discussing that important bill.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration seems to realize suddenly that the amendments to that legislation do not meet the needs of the employees and the purpose of the change is indeed to protect the unemployment insurance fund at the expense of the workers. Since he is aware of the fact that the legislation is rejected by most people, he tries to lessen the impact by having it passed quickly.
Mr. Speaker, the bill under consideration will strike out at once some 50,000 claimants from the rolls. In addition, the new use of the fund is aimed at establishing the concept of pilot work sharing projects which according to the bill are designed for employers faced with financial problems. Under such circumstances, the employer could keep workers for a few days a week and the unemployment insurance fund would make up the difference.
I can hardly conceal my misgivings about the real beneficiaries of those new conditions if the bill is passed and about the dismissals to which companies will surely resort to take advantage of the pilot work sharing projects. However, I am pleased to see that the government has finally understood that it should remove the famous four-week rule which put the unemployed in a corner, and compelled him to accept a temporary job or to lose the right to benefits naturally earned for a former job. Anyhow, he was not free to accept or refuse it, he was automatically excluded. The removal of that stupid rule will provide, I hope, more freedom and scope to the many unemployed.
I will go as far as saying that the whole thrust of this bill is bad but it is my duty as the representative of an area where unemployment is chronic rather than endemic to point out to the government that some amendments to the present legislation will have bad and even disastrous effects in places where unemployment is very serious. The whole country knows that the rate of unemployment is reaching unprecedented highs, particularly in the province of Quebec and the Maritime provinces where unemployment is anywhere from 11.3 per cent to 25 per cent.
There are now 932,000 unemployed in this country. It should be noted that unemployment affects mostly male workers over 25 and young people between 15 and 24. It could be said that the unemployment trend is less obvious in the over 25 group, and the same goes for female workers. Naturally, workers most affected are undoubtedly young people coming

March 30, 1977
Employment and Immigration
onto the labour market every year. The trend toward increased unemployment in that class is unprecedented and too often underrated.
On March 15 last La Presse carried an article by Paul Bennett entitled: Allegations Statistics Canada underrating actual number of young unemployed.
It so happens, Mr. Speaker, that I am in complete agreement with him. Indeed, here is an extract from that article:
The Canadian Council on Social Development blames Statistics Canada for underrating the actual number of young unemployed by using the "actively looking for a job" criterion in its definition of unemployment.
The council starts by recalling alarming statistics on unemployment among young Canadians. Last January, the rate of unemployment reached 13.3 per cent for men and women between the ages of 15 and 24, whereas it barely touched 5.3 per cent for people over 25. On the other hand, for the whole year 1976 the rate of unemployment varied around 12.8 per cent in the 15 to 24 group when it barely exceeded 5 per cent for those over 25. The council goes on to note that the young unemployeds' position relative to their elders has been constantly deteriorating since the early 60's. While the 15-24 age group accounted for two thirds of unemployed in 1964, the proportion is now five to seven.
Mr. Speaker, it is easily seen that unemployment strikes very heavily on our young people in the 15-24 age group. Whether they be educated or not does not matter, unemployment is waiting around the corner. It is no secret anymore that the Canadian economy cannot absorb the huge number of our young people who are available to serve a country where there is so much to be done: senior citizens' centres, housing for every young couple and Canadian family at a price they can afford, road construction, the maintenance and improvement of our transportation systems, and so on.
Mr. Speaker, who but an irresponsible government enslaved to the financial interests of multinational corporations can let so much energy go to waste with such flippancy? It is high time the government responded to the needs of the human being and took the steps to put things back in order. Everything is upside down from coast to coast. There is an urgent need to put things where they belong, so our young people will not be engulfed into something else than the building of our country. Unemployment and inflation are a much more serious dilemma than some members seem to realize.
When unemployment is combined with inflation it represents a risk for any society. The combination of those two factors activates the red light telling us to stop wasting energy and make sure that good sense takes precedence over absurdity.
In La Presse of March 17, editorialist Jean Pelletier wrote, and I quote:
... the Canadian Council on Social Development warned Canada about the explosive political and economic situation that could result if we do not act to reduce excessive unemployment rates among young people. The recent riots in Italy give us an idea of what could happen ...
So it is important that not only the government but also the opposition, management and labour enterprises, as well as experts and economists, study this matter together to avoid a serious social crisis on top of the many difficulties our country is now facing.
I seriously think that it is more than time for this government to consider some answers proposed by our party. I am thinking particularly of pensions at the age of 60, and of
[Mr. Allard.)
course that would be left to the discretion of the person concerned who could choose to leave the labour market and enjoy a well-deserved pension. Pension at 60 would allow a certain number of individuals to retire which would create jobs for newcomers. The guaranteed annual income would also allow many workers to find a job corresponding to their capacities and their training.
Nowadays people are fed up with all the old slogans. They are perfectly aware that the government is not concerned about people and that in our society, money, profit and dollars are the only important values. Workers are always the ones who suffer from inflation and unemployment. Consequently, I should invite the Unemployment Insurance Commission to study the possibility of transferring at the end of the benefit period the two qualifying weeks of the beginning. Also, I ask that the Department of National Revenue and the Unemployment Insurance Commission ensure better coordination in issuing employers' permits. Many members of parliament, like myself, have already gone through several such problems in agriculture, construction or trade as a whole.
Would it not be a good idea, Mr. Speaker, to make sure from the start, before even paying benefits, that the licence the employer holds does authorize him to pay for what are commonly called stamps. This would prevent the Department of National Revenue from saying the claimant was not holding insurable employment and consequently finds himself compelled to pay back any overpayment by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Usually, the claimant has spent his benefits and he is frequently obliged to beg for a loan from the welfare office or his friends, or even from credit cooperatives in order to refund the money to which he thought he was entitled.
Mr. Speaker, a report published in La Presse of January 25, 1977 gives an illustration of how some unemployed proceed to pay back an overpayment to the commission. This article is entitled:
"Pints of blood to refund unemployment insurance."
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, this report states that a 20 year old girl, Vivian Banfield, of Brampton, Ontario, will have to give a pint of blood every six months for two years so as to pay back $685 to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Provincial court Justice John D. Ord ordered her to pay back $350, put her on probation for two years and asked her whether she would agree to give her blood as a public service during this period. She agreed. Miss Banfield was accused of drawing unemployment insurance benefits when she was working. She pleaded guilty. I am all the more convinced that the Unemployment Insurance Act needs to be improved but it must not be done in any way at the expense of workers.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we look at this change in the Unemployment Insurance Act we have to feel somewhat the same as if we had lost a friend. The unemployment insurance structure has become well known over the last few years to all members of parliament. They are
March 30, 1977

pretty well acquainted with it and with the abuses which take place on both sides of the picture. We embark on a new bill knowing there will be many changes, confusing changes, and that it is very unlikely they will be for the advantage either of the workers or of the country.
The minister tells us he is going to save between $225 million and $320 million and that out of this amount about $175 million will come from the change in the benefits; the rest will come about because of the method of payment and the fact that the federal government will not be putting so much into the fund. All this means is that if people do not receive unemployment insurance they will have to get other assistance. We have been through this many times before. We are told that every time there is a change it is for the betterment of someone, but I have yet to see a change that has been of much help except for the last changes when we added sick benefits and maternity benefits. Obviously they were an advantage, though I am still not convinced they should be in the Unemployment Insurance Act; rather, they should be in some legislation under health and welfare because they apply to a much broader segment of the population. People do get injured when not employed or in the labour force, and therefore should receive some benefit.
With most of the changes to the act we have been playing politics and this has been highly detrimental. We split the structure by separating employment from unemployment. We did that last time on a personal basis; we needed to provide a job for a minister so we made that change. I am very happy that this divorce has now ended and that a remarriage is taking place between what I would have thought was a very compatible couple, those who are unemployed and in need of assistance and those who are providing work. It seems to me that that couple should be reunited.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Who is going to pay for the reception?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
The same people who always pay the bill, the general public. Certainly that will be so in this case. It seems to me we are setting up this remarriage without there being much of a marriage contract between the two parties. I am sure there is not a member of the House active in his community who has not been questioned by some of the officials of the Unemployment Insurance Commission or Canada Manpower as to how this marriage will work. The minister says he is taking it to the public by way of participation, that all communities will benefit from this marriage. But I suggest that will not be true.
The only place where you can get job information, Mr. Speaker, is from the computer, and I have yet to find a person who can get information from the computer in one batch. Officials in Manpower are concerned because they do not know what their role will be. They are used to being told, "Hands off UIC; we are divorced from them and do not have anything to do with them. We are no longer friends so do not help fill out any forms or anything". Now the two departments
Employment and Immigration
are being reunited and a lot of very legitimate questions are being asked.
Manpower says it has control over information that is available in their region. If they were smart, though not many of them are, they would have control over job openings in the whole country via the computer. But Manpower are well aware that in many small communities people who work in the UIC do not have access to any information at all. At one time in my community the UIC office went so far as to put in a telex operation, but they found that nothing was coming out at the other end so it was discontinued and they depended on the telephone. Sometimes they found it more advantageous to telephone my office for information than to contact their own offices. This is why they are concerned that this marriage is not going to work. They want to know what responsibilities they will have.
Will they have sufficient information to tell a claimant that if he does certain things benefits will be available for him on such and such a date? Will they have the information required to allow each Manpower centre-and there are more Manpower centres than UIC offices-to answer telephone inquiries from claimants? Will they be able to relate the information they have to potential jobs in the area and make a decision whether those jobs are available?
One of the most frustrating things that can happen to an uninformed claimant when he walks into a UIC office is to be told he has to register at Manpower. If he does register at Manpower he then returns to the UIC office to collect his unemployment insurance. Then a few weeks will go by and he will be told that he has not been looking for work in the area. UIC tell him, "We are told by Manpower centres there are jobs available for you in the area". Then when the claimant goes back to Manpower, his counsellor will say, "I am very sorry, Joe; there are no jobs available for you in this area".
I have never been able to figure out how it is that the Unemployment Insurance Commission ascertains jobs are available when they do not have the machinery for doing so. They say they get the information from Manpower centres, yet the Manpower centres say that no jobs are available. It seems to me that if a person contributes to unemployment insurance, then if he meets the criteria and becomes unemployed, he is entitled to benefits. On the other hand the public must be protected, and if a job is available for someone who is unemployed and is qualified to do the job, then he should take it. It seems to me that if you tell a man that he has not made enough effort to find a job and that you are going to disqualify him, you have to be in a position to tell him that a job is available. If he takes the job, then happily the problem is settled. If there is no job, obviously you cannot disqualify him for not having obtained work. If this marriage produces this kind of result, it will be a great improvement over the present situation.
Much of the criticism I have heard of the UIC relates to benefit control. I know that benefit control officers are turned on and turned off at different times. Every time the public complains about the cost of unemployment insurance, benefit

March 30, 1977
Employment and Immigration
control officers are turned on and they remove a number of people from the rolls. If there are no jobs in the area, then all you are doing is putting these people on municipal welfare rolls. Although there has been criticism of unemployment insurance, I think most members know that if it were not for unemployment insurance in this country, where we have had major unemployment levels for seven or eight years, there would be bankruptcies by the thousand in municipalities across the country. If people who are unemployed cannot get benefits in one way, then they have to get them in another.
In the final analysis, if they cannot get work and cannot get unemployment insurance, then they will have to draw municipal welfare, and in most areas of Canada the municipalities cannot carry the load. Poor communities are mostly in areas of no employment or where there is little more than minimal seasonal employment. Every businessman in the country should be appreciative of unemployment insurance. We would have had a depression that would have made the thirties look like a tea-party had it not been for the amount of money pumped into the program by workers, employers, and to a small extent by the government.
I am not the least bit sympathetic with those who say we have to cut back on unemployment insurance. We have to maintain vigilance. I do not like to hear people in the community say, "I know somebody who is getting unemployment insurance, and they are not entitled to it". I do not like to hear that. When you talk to them, they always say "Oh, Joe told me. It was about Mrs. so-and-so." Nobody ever knows it first-hand. When you follow it up you find that it is not correct.
It is interesting to note that with all the benefit control officers and all the fraud officers that UIC have maintained they have had very few convictions in this country. Many of those convictions were of a marginal nature, where a person was receiving benefits, had gone back to work and they really did not know how to shut him off. I know of a case where a woman got about $900 and thought she had gone through the procedure to shut them off on at least three occasions. She obviously knew she was getting the benefits. The only thing that you could say is that she should not have spent the money. She should have sent it back. She thought the government knew what they were doing. Therefore, she was involved in a fraud case. There are many cases of that nature.
The Conservatives have had a change of heart in another section that is very important.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: We are all heart.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
They have screamed blue murder in this House about abuses of unemployment insurance. The hon. member who seems to be agreeing with that comes from an area where farmers are not unemployed. I would be interested to know whether that particular gentleman would be so sympathetic if there was no rain this summer and farmers were unemployed.
I would be interested to know whether he would be using the

same argument when the farmers ask for help and maybe a farmer in one corner of the township did not have such a bad crop because he was in a swampy area and all the rest were in very serious trouble.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Lang says they have grain stabilization.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Well, Lang's promises of grain stabilization are just about worth the paper they are written on, and not much more. They are saying that we should increase the initial benefit period to qualify from eight weeks to twelve weeks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: That is the qualifying period.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
It sounds reasonable. Eight weeks is not a very long period of time to be working to draw benefits. Twelve weeks is not a very long period, either. In my area I have many people who are trying to raise a family and the only job they get is planting trees and maybe they only get seven, eight or ten weeks of employment. Lands and Forests in Ontario have been trying to give them the qualifying period whenever possible. They will create an extra week of work. If they did not need to plant trees for eight weeks and only needed to plant trees for seven weeks, in many cases they will have planted for the eighth week only to give them the benefit in that area to keep those people.
After the benefit period they draw some benefits. They may get another small period of work, hopefully another eight weeks. It is not because they only work eight weeks to get the advantages of UIC; they can only get that limited amount of work. I know this applies to much of northern Ontario. I imagine it applies to the maritime provinces as well. I think it applies to Quebec the same as it does to northern Ontario. I am sure there are many cases where people would be living on welfare year-round if it were not for the small periods when they can find employment which often qualifies them for UIC.
The Conservatives now say they are going to make exceptions by areas. Well, if there is anything we need less than that to help with the balkanization of Canada, I cannot think of it. Maybe it is another language. It seems to me that the balkanization of this country takes place fast enough without making exceptions. If you come from the maritimes you will only have to work eight weeks; if you come from some place else, you will have to work twelve. Why not make it in the city of Toronto where there is not much unemployment, or in Saskatchewan where there is literally no unemployment? Why not make it 24 weeks, because they obviously have a very high employment figure?
We sometimes fail to realize the benefit to the country that UIC has provided. Because of the contributions it has made it has prevented many storekeepers from going broke. It has prevented many small businesses from going broke in the service industry. It has prevented many of the municipalities throughout all the northern area from going broke. If it did nothing other than that, the government could well afford to throw in the $125 million or some other figure.
March 30, 1977

We are going to try experimental retraining in this country with UIC benefits. I suggest that was not the purpose of UIC. Nobody will ever be told in this country that UIC is helping to carry the educational program in the technical field on a national basis. We will not be told that. We will only be told about the benefits that are being paid out and all the lazy people living on unemployment insurance benefits. We will not be told about the money that the workers are putting up to provide for their own educational systems. Many thought that technical education in this country was free. It looks like the minister is going to reverse that and is going to set up his own educational structure, and UIC is going to pay for it. While I agree it is absolutely necessary, it should be in a special fund rather than under UIC because retraining, unless it is going to be on a national basis and unless it is geared to our ability to provide classifications across the country, will fail to serve much of a purpose in providing for regional unemployment and the difficulties we have with regional unemployment.
The minister may not know that when Manpower was first established one of the things it was going to do was provide employment to a specific person. If you were trained as a secretary, then you were going to be able to get a job as a secretary. Manpower was going to guarantee that you were a secretary when they sent you out. They have not even provided a typewriter in a Manpower centre to check if someone could type or not.
If the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) checks his own staff he will find that almost all of this temporary hiring is done outside of Manpower. He hires very few people through Manpower. Most of it is through Office Overload and the other agencies who can check and tell whether a person is a typist, a secretary, a legal secretary, or what their qualifications are. The private employment section can do that kind of testing. Therefore, it can guarantee when they send somebody out that that person can start work today and can do that kind of job. If the minister will check with his department he will find that most of the people in the job opportunity fields-LIP, LEAP, the Canada Works program or the Youth Works program-have been hired through agencies outside of government agencies. Very few of them come from his agency. He would have to be very dumb if he did not realize that there must be something wrong with the way they select people for specific jobs. If we cannot test a truck driver to see whether he is a truck driver, we are being unfair and pretty stupid. When we send him out, because he has driven a two-ton truck, to drive a Euclid in a mine, he is going to take one look at that truck and say; "I can't drive it", although he is the guy we have sent out as a truck driver.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Send the minister.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
The truck driver knows he is not qualified. If we are going to provide technical training under Manpower, it should be classification training so that we know exactly what the man can do, and we will not send him out on a job that he is incapable of doing. If we do that, the employer will not phone Manpower and ask for another man. If this marriage is
Employment and Immigration
going to be successful, the man who is sent out to a specific job should be reasonably qualified to do that job, or not be sent out. He should be told that there is nothing available. It would make it much easier for the UIC if that were done rather than sending people out who are not qualified for particular jobs.
I know of a person who refused to take a job driving a truck in a mine, and thank God he did. If he had not, he would probably have been killed because he was not qualified to drive a truck. He did not know how to get into it, let alone drive it. If a person refuses to consider a job, the UIC disqualifies him without knowing whether he is capable of doing that job.
I suggest that the minister has an obligation as an individual to look at how the commission works and to make appropriate changes. He should not leave this to bureaucrats who have never worked in a mine, in the bush or done anything except be bureaucrats. They only know the bureaucratic approach, but the minister knows the practical approach. He has worked in mines, he has done manual labour and he knows that if a person is sent out to do the work of an electrician, he had better be an electrician or he will be electrocuted.
The same is true of many other jobs. If unqualified people are sent to do skilled work, they can be replaced very quickly because they will not be around. Employers know this, and they do not accept people who are not qualified. When Manpower does this, it shows how disillusioned it is. The minister knows that less than 50 per cent of the people who are employed are employed through Manpower. Less than 50 per cent are even listed with Manpower. In a given community Manpower does not even know what 50 per cent of the people are employed for. Most Manpower bureaucrats never go out and look at plants to see what they look like, let alone what they do. When Manpower bureaucrats talk about sawyers, they should know that they are not talking about chains-saws. A sawyer is a person who runs the mill. If he is head sawyer in a mill, he has to be highly skilled because the whole operation depends on him. If he is not competent, the company will be broke before many days go by. When a man is sent out, he has to know the job, and the employer wants to know that he knows the job. Therefore, a technical selection has to be carried out by the department with trained people making inspections of what people are registering for.
This bill amounts to nothing but bureaucratic jargon. It does not say what it means and it does not mean what it says. If the French version of this bill contains as much gobbledegook as the English version, bilingualism will be set back centuries. Ten interpretations can be taken from one paragraph. The minister knows that because he is a practical person.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: He is not practical.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
He is a lawyer.

March 30, 1977
Employment and Immigration

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, but he had ability when he was going to college. I knew his dad quite well, and he was not rich. He was a doctor, but he was not rich. His dad probably made him work for a living. I know the minister has some experience in the mines of northern Ontario, and that is practical experience. Even though he is a lawyer, he probably likes to read a piece of legislation and not have to compare his interpretation with that of two other lawyers. A year or so ago a fellow asked me to fill out an unemployment insurance card for him. It was a long form. I took one look at it and told him that he should have someone from downtown fill it out for him. I did not know how to fill it out. Every question had two possible answers, and no matter how it was answered there could be problems.
For example, if one question was, "Have you stopped beating your wife yet" and you answered "No", that could mean you still were. If the answer was "Yes", that could mean that you once did beat her. Most of the questions were like that. One question was, "Do you have transportation?" To most people, transportation means a bus, but in my part of the country it means an automobile. If people in my part of the country do not have automobiles, they do not have transportation. If the buses do not go where you go, you do not have transportation. However, people who work in plants drive automobiles, and if a person knows what shift he is on, on the second day that person will darned well have transportation. On the first day that person may have to take a taxi. But when a person does not even have the hope of a job, he certainly does not know where that job is to be located. It is hard to decide whether a person has transportation before knowing what or where the job is going to be. If I am asked if I have transportation, I do not know. I assume I have. Once I had a job but no car. There was no bus service, but I had transportation. On the second day of work I was able to get a ride with someone who had a car.
Do I tell these bureaucrats that I have transportation? They will probably ask me if I have a car, and I will have to say "no", and then they will say I do not have transportation. Then I will have to say, "I guess you are right, because I don't have a horse either". In every case, if an applicant makes a wrong answer he is disqualified.
They ask how much money an applicant wants. That seems to be a very simple question. If I had a previous job and was paid $5 an hour, I would say I would work for $5 an hour. I might take $4 or I might work for $3.50, but that is not the question. The question is how much money an applicant wants. If an applicant goes the other way and says he wants $10 an hour, he is disqualified because there are no jobs paying $10. These benefit control officers are great people! In one week they can wipe out half the people on unemployment insurance. It does not matter that the next week they might be over at the municipal welfare office; the bureaucrats do what they are told to do. When they are told to reduce the roll, they reduce it.
This bill does not have to be as complicated as it is. If an applicant appeals and there is dissent, the applicant can go to the umpire. Why should matters be taken to the umpire unless there is a question of legal interpretation? Things have been

changed and there is now only one referee, and he can be as biased as he wants to be. When there were three the situation was not so bad. The three of them would look at the precedents and make a decision. Applicants should be able to go to the umpire only if a matter of law is involved. If it is a matter of principle involved, that could be solved by legislative action. Then it would be possible to go to the umpire, the minister could look at the umpire's decisions, and if he found a series of consistent rulings on a matter of principle he could change the regulations and solve that problem. Then the umpire would not have to be bothered with that particular principle any more.
Once the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) went to his representative on the board of referees and told him he would go before the labour council and have him kicked off the board if he did not dissent from bad decisions. From then on that representative dissented from all decisions, and that was iust as ridiculous.
I did not become involved with any of those matters because they took place in Sudbury, which is far away from my people. However, the hon. member sent 13 cases to me at one time and I won 12 of them. Hon. members can ask the director of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and he will confirm what I am saying. The director went on television, used those 12 cases and said that the argument was made to the benefit control officer that his interpretation was not necessarily correct. I won 11 or 12 of those 13 cases. I have not seen any since. They are not sent to me any more and I do not know if there is still a problem. I certainly do not stir up cases. I deal with them only when they come to me. I am not looking for any.
The point I am making is that if we look at these things impartially, without trying to get rid of people, and if we look at them fairly and honestly, knowing that there are no jobs available in an area and knowing that no transportation is available, applications should be accepted and people should not have to go to the umpire. These particular cases went through the bureaucratic machinery and they were solved.
I suggest that many difficulties of the average person are with bureaucrats whose only job is to figure out the language. I know that proper legal terms must be used and that it makes a great deal of difference whether you use "will", "shall", "should", "must", "might", or "may". But really it is not the main function of UIC to provide benefits to the unemployed with the least offence to them. It is part of our responsibility as government to provide work.
Let us consider such employment agencies as Office Overload. I have a son who hired people for a big electronic company in Toronto. Among others he hired "think engineers". A "think engineer" would come to an office, watch the wall for a while and think about the problem. If, in a couple of weeks, he did not come up with an answer, the company would let him go and telephone the agency to send in another "think engineer", or he might think about the wrong problem and you would get something out of him that you could not use. You hired him because he belonged to a professional pool of "think
March 30, 1977

engineers". You needed him to solve a particular problem, not as a permanent employee.
Until the Manpower centres can provide people in specific categories, such as a rough carpenter, a finish carpenter or a bench carpenter, they will not be doing their job properly. The centre must provide the appropriate person for the employer. The employer does not want to interview a whole lot of people. One lawyer told me that he needed a legal secretary and he interviewed six different girls from Manpower. It is pretty simple to hire a legal secretary, but that was not the case. He made a good suggestion. What Manpower did was to put his professional card on the board stating that a legal secretary was wanted. He told them that it would be better if they were to reprint or photostat his card and pin it up in Loblaw's or Steinberg's because many people go by the bulletin boards in these stores. He said that in the Manpower office only four or five people went by that board on which his card was pinned. Unless there are many people looking for jobs, by going to the board, or many employers looking for employees, we are not providing a proper employment service.
I remember the time when one used to pay to get a job. I remember going to Timmins in 1940 to apply for a job in the mine. The guy wanted five bucks to talk to you about the job. I did not have five bucks at the time and I gave him a really good story. I got the job partly because I was a farm boy. In those times five bucks almost always got you a job. There were not too many five bucks going around then. You would not save that much money in a week at that time, but when you paid the money you got the job. We are paying the Minister of Manpower and Immigration to provide employment, but he is not supplying the jobs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: He wants more money.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I honestly believe that unemployment insurance should be under the Department of Manpower. I believe we had a good system in Canada when we did not use computers. We had people instead of computers. Many hon. members will not remember it, but when unemployment insurance was first started, all the information was contained on a card, every contribution you paid and how much you were going to be paid every week. When you walked into the office, they got out the card and told you immediately how much money you were entitled to, so much a week, and they would hand you the money. But before you got the money you would have to go over to the other side of the room and ask if there were any jobs available. If a job was offered, you had to take it. If there was no job available, you went back and got your money. When the money was all gone, they started another card.
It may have been an amateurish system. It may have been damned humiliating for highbrow people to have to walk into an office and get the dole after having asked for a job. But that does not worry me and it certainly does not worry the people I represent. They would be damned happy to have that system if it were a more honest one. Because what we have now is not honest. A person thinks he is looking for a job, but UIC says
Employment and Immigration
he is malingering and guilty of all kinds of bad practices because he is not following their regulations.
In my area there is a sawmill employing 40 people. If you worked in that sawmill you know how many men are employed and you know there are no vacancies. What is the point of asking for a job there three times a week? What is the point of asking for a job in the local hotel if you cannot add or subtract? But unemployment insurance says that you have to go there and ask. What is the point of asking for a job in the local restaurant if you have a long beard and are filthy? They will not give you a job, but you have to go and ask. What is the point of going to the liquor store when you know that in Ontario you have to be a lifelong Conservative to get a job there? If you are a Liberal or a member of the NDP, you have no chance.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Is that not phony? To me it seems totally idiotic. Surely there are half a dozen people who know that in a certain community there are no jobs available. A guy looking for a job had worked all his life and is willing, but he is not very bright. We would give him a job if one was available, but there is no job. Why should he be made to suffer the indignity of looking for a job when everyone knows there is no job available? Surely to God under the new system Manpower should make an effort.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: There is no hope of that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: The system will only work if we quit fooling around with peripheral matters and get down to providing employment service where the guy gets off his fanny, walks around to the local plant and suggests to the employer, "You can use a guy to clean this up". He might say, "If we send you a man, you could give him that job". Until we do that, this program will not work. These changes are in the main to satisfy the very small fringe element which believes that unemployment insurance should be stopped. These changes are for their benefit. But there are so many changes that could be made for the benefit of the country to provide jobs, to make jobs available which an employer might not even know he can provide. The one provision in this act which is worse than all others is the change in the benefit period. In my area, if people can work for 12 weeks they will draw unemployment insurance. If they can only get jobs for 8 weeks, it would be better if they could draw benefits on that than get welfare from the municipal welfare office.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to use this afternoon to register, in the second reading stage of Bill C-27, some of my concerns as a member of parliament from the Atlantic provinces. I cannot help but express my views, give praise where due and make suggestions in other areas. I am sure everyone is pleased to see the integration of manpower, unemployment and immigration services. This integration would produce a new organization. This will produce a new organization capable of providing, as the minister calls it, a one-stop service to the people. Obvious-

March 30, 1977
Employment and Immigration
ly, this is a proper step. Why should people who are seeking UIC benefits and who must register at Manpower as a prerequisite for benefits, have to go to two different places? This way, the same person who dealt with the benefits will also see the problems involved with finding employment. They can now work together to solve the existing problems of long-term employment.
The servicing which presently exists leaves a lot to be desired. Why can cheques not be sent out faster? Why do returns go through three areas before they reach head office? The terminology has been mentioned earlier, and I agree with this. Let us hope this will be a one-step service and that it will not increase the amount of work the unemployed person has to do in order to get benefits.
The new supporting department of employment and immigration, we are told, will be responsible for strategic policy development, program evolution, labour market research and information services. If this means we are going to do away with relying on inaccurate statistics for South Western Nova I think this alone would be an improvement. My only suggestion to the minister would be to make sure that we are not duplicating service and that this department will be made to produce and really promote the closest possible co-operation between labour market policies and progress and the government's over-all economic and social strategies.
I am glad to see the minister hopes that integration will lead to the simplification of documentation required of the public. I am pleased, as well, to see that the penalty for working more than four weeks will be removed. In other words, the person drawing UIC benefits who finds work for more than four weeks and then becomes unemployed in the past has automatically become disqualified from re-establishing his benefit period. In areas where work is seasonal this has been very detrimental to the employment picture. There are other good points such as the transfer of benefits. If a person is owed benefits and they are slow in coming in, he can go to the municipal authority and transfer receipt of UIC benefits to the municipal assistance authority. I am sure this will alleviate a lot of hardship. There is also the developmental use of UIC funds which I hope to be able to talk about before I finish.
As I have stated, these are some reforms, but there are others which have not been attended to. In the administrative areas there is the use of unemployment insurance versus the guaranteed annual income. There are wives who, if they work for their husbands, cannot collect unemployment insurance. In other words, the shucker in Newfoundland cannot work for her husband, the scalloper, and so must work for her friend's husband. There are also wives whose husbands run a one-man business yet they cannot work for him and receive benefits. There is also no reform reducing the amount of benefit after a certain period of time. There is the woman on maternity leave who has to wait three weeks for benefits even though her child is due two days after she commences maternity leave. These are just some of the concerns that I have not seen dealt with in

the reforms. I also have concerns when I look at the implications and implementation of this bill.
If we go back to the federal budget of May, 1976, we find that the government announced its intention to reform the scope and administration of the unemployment insurance program in Canada. Specific proposals included recasting of the benefit structure and an increase of the minimum entrance requirement for the program from 8 weeks to 12 weeks of insured employment. Reaction to the proposals focused on the number of individuals who would be affected by increased entrance requirements.
In the next few minutes I should like to register my concerns in terms of claimants who would have been affected had this been law in 1976, give a projection of how it would affect the claimants in 1977 and the effects of the reduction of benefit in the maritimes as well as in my own area. In this time period I am referring to the Unemployment Insurance Commission's "Comprehensive Review of the Unemployment Insurance Program in Canada, February, 1977", which I will refer to as "the review" for purposes of this discussion.
At page K54 the review states that a total of 330,000 claimants throughout the year would be affected by the increase in the qualifying period. It is estimated that at any point in time in 1976 there was an average of 100,000 beneficiaries with 8 to 11 weeks of insured employment. The minister and the review have assumed that 50 per cent of the 8 to 11-weekers shown at page K57 would be able to find additional insured employment or continue at their present employment, in order to qualify for benefits at the 12-weeks' entrance requirement. Had the 12-week extension been implemented in 1976, roughly 50,000 people nationally would never have received benefits at any point in time. Going back to the 330,000 claimants, if you take 30 per cent of them as being affected you come to 100,000 beneficiaries who had 8 to 11 weeks of insured employment. As stated by the minister, if you take 50 per cent of these being able to find the additional weeks, there is 50 per cent left-in other words, 50,000 people. If you look at page K58 you find details per province. As far as Nova Scotia goes, 2,600 of the 50,000 would be affected at any one time, and 9,800 in all the Atlantic provinces.
Let us look at the claimants affected by increased entrance requirements and give a projection for 1977 of the number of claimants affected by the 12-week entrance requirement. This is the counterpart of what I have just said and what is shown at page K54 of the review. Based on the assumptions required to derive what I am assuming, that is, that we should have to take a labour force growth of 2 per cent in 1977, an unemployment rate of 8 per cent in 1977, a constant ratio of unemployed to beneficiary population between 1976 and 1977 and the same proportion of beneficiaries in each province between 1976 and 1977, what do we come down to? We come down to an estimate that there would be an average of 117,328 beneficiaries with 8 to 11 weeks of insured employment. If we again assume that 50 per cent of the 8 to 11-weekers in 1977 will find additional insured weeks in order to qualify for benefits at the higher entrance requirement, a total of 58,664
March 30, 1977

persons will be unable to receive benefits at any given point during 1977. In other words, implementation of the 12-week qualifying period would disqualify from UIC benefits about 59,000 potential beneficiaries in 1977. Of these, roughly 11,500 would be residents of the Atlantic provinces.
Let us consider how this reduction in benefit levels will affect the Atlantic provinces. Total benefits under the proposed amendment would be reduced by both increased entrance requirements and by the introduction of the new three-phase benefit structure for those individuals who receive benefits. In other words, under the present structure somebody with 8 weeks of employment receives 32 weeks of benefits. Under the three-phase benefit structure there would be no such assistance. At present, after 12 insured weeks of employment the claimant is entitled to 32 benefit weeks. He would also be entitled to 32 benefit weeks under the three-phase benefit structure. Of course, I am referring to what would happen if one considers that the Nova Scotia unemployment rate is 10 per cent, as opposed to the national unemployment rate of 8 per cent. After the twentieth week of insured earning, the present structure would provide one more week of benefit than the new three-phase system would provide.
The major difference between the two structures concerns the loss of benefits for the 8 to 11 -weekers, a group which is of considerable size in the Atlantic provinces. Putting it in round numbers, one could say that there would be 59,000 potential beneficiaries across Canada and 11,500 in the Atlantic provinces. Those figures are based on the labour force survey. I have my doubts about the validity of the labour force survey.
The UIC review also assesses the financial impact of the 12-week entrance requirement when combined with the new benefit structure. For instance, the study found that at a national unemployment rate of 8 per cent, the total savings accruing from the new proposals in 1976 dollars would be in the $250 million to $300 million range. These figures no doubt assume that a number of the 8 to 11-weekers would qualify for benefits under the 12-week minimum. The government's share of the total would be between $175 million and $210 million, the remainder being saved by employers and employees.
For 1977 an estimate of total savings would be in the $325 million to $390 million range, given an increase in insured earnings of 13 per cent and provided the number of beneficiaries increases to 58,664, or 59,000 in round numbers, or is about 17 per cent greater than the number in 1976. In terms of the loss of funds to the Atlantic provinces, if it is assumed that their loss is in proportion to the number of beneficiaries with 8 to 11 weeks in 1977-11,496-then the loss would be between $63 million and $76 million in 1977. Altsrnatively, a figure of $62 million in 1977 is suggested if it is assumed that the 11,496 beneficiaries in Atlantic Canada received an average weekly benefit of $104 in 1977. In December, 1976, the average weekly benefit paid in the four Atlantic provinces was $92. In either case, the economies of the Atlantic provinces
Employment and Immigration
will be seriously affected by the reduction in benefits, in human as well as in dollar terms.
How will all this affect South Western Nova? The picture looks pretty bleak. Let us assume that between November, 1975, and October, 1976, altogether 44,290 persons were registered at the Yarmouth UIC office. Therefore, on average 3,690 people per month during the 12-month period were registered with the office. Assume, further, that 30 per cent of those registered are 8 to 11 weekers, as the minister suggested. That means that 1,107 people per month were 8 to 11 weekers. Let us divide that figure in half because supposedly half will be able to find work. We see, therefore, that 554 people will not be able to receive benefits. If you multiply that figure by 104-I am thinking of benefits of $104 a week, one readily sees that the government will save $57,616 per week. Multiply that figure by 52, there being 52 weeks in the year, and the result is $2,996,032. That amount will not flow into the area serviced by the Yarmouth UIC office.
What does all this mean? According to the 1971 census the population of South Western Nova was 62,177 persons. In February, 1976, 7,607 people were registered with the local UIC office. Clearly, the new program will hurt in the sense that funds allocated in the past for job creation projects such as LIP, and now we have Canada Works, were determined by the unemployment rate which was based on the labour force survey. As you know, the labour force is made up of people 15 years of age and older who are working or have actively been looking for employment in the last four weeks. The labour force survey says that one is employed if one has done any work in the previous reference week.
The unemployment rate in 1976 in economic region 24, which includes South Western Nova, was 9.2 per cent. But if you consider only those registered at UIC offices, say between November, 1975, and October, 1976, the picture will be entirely different. We note that unemployment in the winter is high and that it goes down to low levels in the summer.
What happens if you accept the unemployment rate as set out in the labour force survey? As I said, that survey defines "employed" as any work performed in the past reference week. What happens is this: if a fisherman works even one hour of one day during the reference week, according to the labour force survey he was employed that week. But if he does not work, he is not included in the labour force, because he cannot search for a job in that occupation. Such considerations apply to all seasonal workers, be they loggers, people working in the tourist industry, fish plant workers or other workers doing seasonal work. The statistics would also show, because of the seasonal nature of employment in the area, that employment declines in the summer.
Much has been said about the participation rate. What is it? The participation rate is the number of people in the labour force over the total number of persons 15 years old and older in any given area. I think the participation rate should be taken into consideration when one considers the numbers of people registered at UIC offices. I say this because I am trying to show that there is considerable difference between the

March 30, 1977
Employment and Immigration
Statistics Canada labour force survey and the number of registered UIC claimants. In addition, not only do those figures differ considerably, but if you are going to undertake job creation programs on the basis of the labour force survey it is apparent that an area like mine will be hurt terribly.
I am trying to show that the 8 to 11-weekers in my area will be affected by this proposed amendment. The participation rate for economic region 24, and that includes South Western Nova, was 51 per cent. For the province it was 55.2 per cent. This is rates of employment in the labour force during the summer months when people are employed. In January, 1976, the participation rate for economic region 24 was 45 per cent, whereas for Nova Scotia it was 51.9 per cent.
As I said, the Canada Works program was established to create jobs. However, South Western Nova was given the lowest allocation after Halifax. From November, 1975, to October, 1976, a total of $16,881,000 in unemployment insurance benefits was paid out of the Yarmouth UIC office. In all of Nova Scotia for the same period a total of $147,042,000 was paid out. This indicates that the amount of money being paid out of the UIC office does not show up in terms of the labour force survey studies and the unemployment rate.
Canada Works replaces the Local Initiatives Program. Given the same set of facts, my area received the lowest allocation outside of Halifax. How, then, can I accept for the 8 to 11-weekers the amendments and the labour force survey when at the same time no money is coming back into that area? I will deal with that in a minute.
The Canada Works program this year is based on three criteria: the unemployment rate in the labour force for Nova Scotia; the total number of claimants registered from December, 1975, to November, 1976, in Nova Scotia; and the 1971 census per county in Nova Scotia of unemployed, which incidentally is based on the same definition as the labour force survey. It should be noted that figures for A and B are the same in Nova Scotia in 1976. For this reason I rejected the validity of the Local Initiatives Program allocations for South Western Nova and I must again reject the validity of the allocations for the Canada Works and Young Canada Works programs for my area.
I wish to deal with the number of unemployment insurance claimants for January, February and March, 1976. In January, 1976, there were 6,355 claimants registered. I ask hon. members to bear in mind that my population total is 62,000 or so people. If you take 25 per cent of that figure as being persons able to work, and say that in January there were 6,355 people unemployed, there were not too many people not looking for assistance from the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The figure for February was 7,607, and March 7,408. I agree that I have an area of seasonal employment.
I do not think this is the time to go into the labour force survey. Why, when the Manpower offices have unemployment insurance statistics as well as Manpower registrations, do we have to use a labour force survey that is discriminatory in a

sense that it is the rural versus the urban. In economic region 24, for example, it is rural areas for the most part. As well, it is seasonal versus permanent jobs. I wish to put on record the fact that economic region 24 comprises all of Digby, Yarmouth, Shelburne, Queens and Lunenburg counties. The preliminary 1976 census shows that the growth in economic region 24 was 1.9 per cent, and for all of Nova Scotia it was 3 per cent. If you withdraw Lunenburg county from economic region 24, you will see very little growth in South Western Nova. The economic growth in Lunenburg county was approximately 4.5 per cent. Again for the record, South Western Nova comprises the bottom part of Annapolis county, which has no town as such. There is Annapolis Royal, which is a town of approximately 850 people. It also comprises all of Digby and Yarmouth counties, half of Shelburne county and the municipality of Barrington. The UIC office in Yarmouth takes in Yarmouth, Shelburne and Digby counties. I realize that some of these statistics can be questioned.
With regard to the labour force survey, an article in the March 2 Gazette indicates that unemployment figures released by Statistics Canada represent only a fraction of the actual number of persons without jobs who want to work. The survey was undertaken by the University of Regina and was funded by the Department of Manpower. I hope that department will act on the results of the survey.
What will be the effect of an increase from 8 to 12 weeks for insured earnings and the decrease in the benefit period? The government is asking an area like South Western Nova to find employment both during the 8 to 12-week period and the reduced benefit. In other words, "A" will now have to find 12 weeks. Before, if "A" found 12 weeks, he got 29 weeks of benefits. Now "A" will get 26 weeks for 12 weeks. I must speak of my concerns about this policy because I do not see any money to provide these targeted people who need work to bring them up to 12 weeks and to get them back. I am waiting to see what the designated work programs will be. The community as a whole will suffer because there will be less UIC money circulating around the area. How much will be cut back, no one knows. I have given estimates, but they are only estimates. If one looks at last year's figures, one has to wonder. I take a certain amount of confidence from the minister's statement of October 21, 1976. I quote from page 340 of Hansard'.
In 1977-78, the first full year of our five-year employment strategy, we plan to invest in the neighbourhood of $350 million beyond our regular expenditures on manpower programs. Over that five-year period much of the incremental funding for the employment strategy will come from changes in the unemployment insurance legislation. In the first full year savings to the government from the legislative changes will be about $10 million, but future savings will be even greater. Because unemployment insurance savings will rise as unemployment declines, we are looking at costs and resources averaged over five years. It is generally expected that, if parliament approves the changes 1 shall propose to the Unemployment Insurance Act, reduced government contributions to the unemployment insurance account will offset the extra costs of this employment strategy.
We can take a certain amount of consolation, I suppose, if one fits all the criteria, but up until now my area has had very

March 30, 1977

little in terms of creating jobs. I should like to say a few words on job creation since this represents the other part of the UIC amendments-the money going into job creation. I would suggest to the minister and to the officials of the department that they should consider looking at areas to see what resources are available. Look at the municipalities. They need sewers and water systems, housing, land clearance for future use. We-now have oil exploration off the coast of Nova Scotia. I wonder how many people will be trained by Manpower. I wonder how many will come in from the United States, from across Canada or from the United Kingdom to take jobs. Perhaps one of the terms of Petro-Canada on entering into any contract should be that they hire locally, that they register with Manpower and state what jobs will become available.
Look at our 200-mile limit. We have fish, yet on the finished product we have a tariff. We discourage finishing the product. I should like to see the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce establish markets for fish. I should like to see new factories. Now that we are in control of waters within the 200-mile limit, I should like to see more local people hired and trained. As well, I should like to see these factories operating for longer periods.
We have woodland. Why cannot it be cleared? Why cannot we reforest our land? I should like to see local tendering on government contracts encouraged. I should like to see encouragement given to groups of people for this purpose. I am also aware that in the information papers on the employment and reorganization legislation the minister goes into the development uses of unemployment insurance funds. I welcome the additional training projects. I welcome pilot projects for job creation programs, community-oriented programs where people will feel they have a chance to look at the work. However, I have waited a long time to see a community employment program come into the area, yet we have had "New Start", the "Adult Modules" and other such organizations. We have never seen the rest.
However, I will repeat the question: Will these programs and will this money be designated toward the 8 to 11-weekers? In my humble opinion, the statistics we have had to deal with in the past make me doubtful. I do not know. I am looking forward to seeing what the committee and the report stage are going to bring forth. When I see the estimate for 1977-close to $3 million, using the designated figures-I wonder, especially when I get $190,000 on Canada Works in the first phase. One has to look at the implications of the bill not only in terms of the individuals who will be affected, that is, the 8 to 11-weekers, but also at the community level. I am thinking of those who will have to find jobs for, or support, these people. People will also lose money, as I have said, $62 million in the Atlantic provinces if we go by the projected figure of 50 per cent of the people being affected in the Atlantic provinces.
I look forward to getting the answers to these questions. There are good points in this bill-the transfer of benefits, the sick benefits, the integration of the manpower, unemployment and immigration services, as well as being able to work without being penalized for working during a benefit period. I
Employment and Immigration
cannot understand how we could not have had this before now. Last year we had other changes, and they are working. We had the disqualifying period lengthened for persons who quit. We had maternity benefits, but, as I say, they did not go far enough. When a woman quits two days before entering hospital, surely she does not have to wait three weeks before getting her benefits; you have already deprived her, when she is going back to work in three months, of three weeks. I must say that I look forward to a solution, whether it is in awareness of the problem that the reduced benefit period and the increased qualifying insured weeks will have, whether it is an increase in job creation, or whether it is assurances that go further and which will affect the target groups.
I should also like to say that perhaps the labour force survey should be thrown out and unemployment insurance commission statistics and Department of Manpower statistics be used. If we are paying it out from there, why are not those statistics relevant? Why depend on the labour force survey? I look forward to seeing what will develop in the committee. I have tried to register my concern in terms of the money and job creation for the 8 to 11-weekers as well as what it will do to the area, not only to the Atlantic provinces but to a constituency such as mine which is a seasonal job area. Unless job creation can come out with jobs that are going to be extended, and unless it takes into account some of the local people, instead of starting here in Ottawa and dishing it out to regions, these programs cannot but hurt a great many people.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before calling it six o'clock I should just like to say to the minister that maybe he now appreciates to a degree the monster he created when he imposed closure on this particular piece of legislation and in effect brought Liberals into the debate to make 40-minute speeches. He has suffered through it, and so has every other member of the House, trying to follow the hon. member for South Western Nova (Miss Campbell) who made indirectly one of the most vicious attacks on the government which could possibly be made, because she said, in effect, as far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned, "We rely on unemployment, not on employment, to keep people with some money in their pockets". That is a terrible condemnation of the government or of a government anywhere in a country as great as this one.
